findings.summary: Capacity section lists the same numbers twice, first as a loose fragment list and then as a table, so the page repeats itself and the loose fragments are hard to follow.
findings.evidence: 100M URLs/month / new writes / ~40 writes/s / ~400/s at 10x peak / x100 reads / 10B redirects/month / ~4,000 QPS / ~40,000 at peak
findings.fix: Keep the Estimate | Math | Result table and drop the fragment list, or turn it into a labelled writes-to-reads diagram.

findings.summary: The 'Size the cache from daily traffic' callout packs several ideas into one block of prose.
findings.evidence: Hot set = 20% of daily redirects (70M x 500 B = 35 GB), not 20% of all stored links, which would be 600 GB.
findings.fix: Split into two one-line bullets: the correct basis (20% of daily redirects = 35 GB) and the wrong basis (20% of stored links = 600 GB).

findings.summary: KGS is used in the components table before it is defined on page 4.
findings.evidence: ID generator | Unique integer per new URL | Counter ranges or KGS
findings.fix: Expand KGS here (pre-generated key service) and say that page 4 covers it, or use plain wording until page 4.

findings.summary: The claim that 6-character codes are too tight for 6B URLs overstates the problem.
findings.evidence: 6 chars | 62^6 | 56.8B | Too tight for 6B URLs plus retries
findings.fix: 6B URLs fill only about 10.5% of 62^6. Say 6 chars is workable for counter or KGS but leaves little collision headroom for hash or random codes, or explain the 7-char choice by headroom and growth instead of 'too tight'.

findings.summary: The 6-character row calls 62^6 "too tight" for 6B URLs, but 56.8B is about 9x larger, so the verdict misleads.
findings.evidence: 6 chars | 62^6 | 56.8B | Too tight for 6B URLs plus retries
findings.fix: State the real reason for 7 chars: 6B URLs would use about 10.6% of 62^6, which leaves little room to grow or for sparse random allocation. 7 chars brings that down to 0.17%. Or drop the "too tight" wording.

findings.summary: The Python snippet appears before the idea behind it is stated, and the one-line explanation is placed after the code.
findings.evidence: A = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" ... prepending replaces the final reverse
findings.fix: State the idea first (build the code from remainders, prepending each character), then show the code.

findings.summary: The 'Remember' callout and the metrics bullets are mixed together, so the metrics read as part of the Remember box.
findings.evidence: Remember / Unique, short, and unguessable pull against each other... / Track the code length distribution / Track keyspace used % of 62^7 / Alert at 50% of 62^7 used
findings.fix: Put the metrics under their own 'Metrics' heading, separate from the Remember callout.

findings.summary: The 'Sequential base62 leaks' section lists the problem but the fix bullet ('random-looking keys') is not tied to a mechanism, which the next page then covers.
findings.evidence: Fix: random-looking keys, not raw counters
findings.fix: Add a pointer such as 'see KGS on the next page', or name the mechanism in the bullet.

findings.summary: Several bullets hold more than one idea, and the SQL snippet comes at the end under a 'Mistakes' heading, with the risk stated only after it.
findings.evidence: Collisions grow past ~1M links (birthday bound on 7 chars) / Needs a distributed counter: a single one is a bottleneck and a SPOF
findings.fix: Split each into one-idea bullets, and state the 'random without a guard' risk before showing the SQL.

findings.summary: The hash collision-loop diagram has a duplicated retry edge and the 'Counter' section uses a different wording from the 'Counter ranges' diagram, so the flow is harder to follow.
findings.evidence: Add salt, rehash --retry--> Code free?
findings.fix: Draw one linear loop (hash, check, free: store; taken: salt and rehash back to hash) and use the same term 'counter ranges' in both places.

findings.summary: The 301 vs 302 text mixes the recommendation with caching details, so the decision rules read as dense bullets, and the code is shown before its one-line idea.
findings.evidence: Analytics and expiry needed → 302 (or 307), or a 301 with a short private max-age as Bitly does
findings.fix: Split into separate bullets: 'Need analytics or expiry: 302', 'Alternative: 301 with short private max-age', 'Pure SEO: 301'. State the idea before the http block.

findings.summary: The redirect flow diagram uses '3xx' while the later sections discuss 301 and 302 as the choice, and the 'Pitfall' is a prose paragraph.
findings.evidence: 301 is hard to undo / A wrongly-cached permanent redirect with a long max-age stays in browsers for months. You cannot recall it, so never ship a long 301 max-age for links you may change or expire.
findings.fix: Turn the pitfall into short bullets (what happens, why it cannot be undone, the rule), and annotate the diagram 'per the chosen status'.

findings.summary: The data model says a null expires_at means the default TTL, but the expiry check treats null as no expiry.
findings.evidence: expires_at | Nullable; null means default TTL  vs  "expires_at set and in the past? --no--> 302 to long_url" and page 1 "Default TTL when none is given: 5 years"
findings.fix: Either write expires_at = created_at + 5 years at insert time when none is supplied, or state that null means the link never expires and drop the default-TTL wording.

findings.summary: The expiry flow and data model disagree about null expires_at and the 5-year default TTL.
findings.evidence: expires_at | Nullable; null means default TTL  versus  expires_at set and in the past? --no--> 302 to long_url
findings.fix: Resolve the default at create time by storing created_at plus 5 years in expires_at, or add a branch to the flow that applies the default TTL when expires_at is null.

findings.summary: Page mixes the expiry and alias topics under a title that lists aliases first, and the 410 status appears in the expiry flow but the 'Failure' section and API table repeat the unique-index rule several times.
findings.evidence: Insert-or-fail is atomic: no check-then-insert race / let the unique index decide, never SELECT first / No check-then-insert / A SELECT before the INSERT lets both users pass.
findings.fix: State the unique-index rule once and refer back to it; keep the concurrent-claim diagram and trim the repeated bullets.

findings.summary: The 'Charset' and 'Length' alias rules are bare fragments listed without a heading, so they look like part of the status table.
findings.evidence: Length 4-30 chars / Charset [A-Za-z0-9_-] / Case-sensitive: Sale and sale are different codes
findings.fix: Add a 'Alias rules' label above those bullets.

findings.summary: The failure-mode bullets are grouped under a code-block heading rather than a labelled section, and the 'Event' schema is embedded in a prose bullet.
findings.evidence: Redirect returns first, then publishes a click event to Kafka / Event: {code, ts, ip, user_agent, referrer}
findings.fix: Split into a pipeline diagram caption and a separate 'Event fields' line; label the Kafka-down block as 'Failure: Kafka down' in its own section.

findings.summary: Caching hot 302 targets at the edge contradicts the click-analytics and expiry guarantees.
findings.evidence: Cache 301s, and only hot 302 targets with a short TTL / Edge hits never reach the API, so redirect p99 stays under 50 ms
findings.fix: Note that edge hits are not counted in analytics (or must emit click events from the edge) and that expiry is only enforced at the next TTL refresh. Do not recommend caching 301s without the short max-age caveat.

findings.summary: The 'Protect the DB' callout is one long sentence that holds two ideas (stampede and scan) and the cache-sizing math is repeated in a table and in a closing 'Cache targets' list.
findings.evidence: Everything else waits on the one refill for a stampede, and a scan hits the negative key for 60 s instead of the DB.
findings.fix: Split into two bullets (stampede: one refill; scan: negative key) and drop the duplicated targets list or merge it with the table.

findings.summary: Edge-cache bullets mix 301 and 302 caching rules in one line, which contradicts the earlier advice to avoid long-cached redirects.
findings.evidence: Cache 301s, and only hot 302 targets with a short TTL
findings.fix: Split into separate bullets and note that CDN-cached 301s cannot be revoked, consistent with page 5.

findings.summary: Terminology for shards and nodes shifts: the sizing table says '3 shards x 1 TB' and '6 shards x 1 TB' and then '18 nodes', and the ring diagram says 'Shard 1 of 6', so a skimmer must work out how shards map to nodes.
findings.evidence: 6 shards x (1 primary + 2 replicas) | 18 nodes
findings.fix: Add a one-line definition: 1 shard = 1 primary + 2 replicas = 3 nodes, so 6 shards = 18 nodes.

findings.summary: The replication section holds long bullets with two ideas each, and the 'Fresh link 404' callout repeats the fix already stated just above.
findings.evidence: Async copy keeps the write path fast, but replicas can lag / Fix: read the primary right after create, replicas for everything else / Created links must work at once. After POST, the first reads go to the primary, never a lagging replica.
findings.fix: Split the lag bullet, and keep either the fix bullet or the callout, not both.

findings.summary: The scaling page holds a long run of bullets with several ideas each (regions, key ranges, abuse), and the interview answers are dense one-line prose.
findings.evidence: Reads: active-active in every region, each with a regional cache / Writes: go to a home region / Each region owns its own key range, so IDs never clash
findings.fix: Group under 'Regions' and 'Abuse' headings with one idea per bullet, and shorten each interview answer to a short bullet list.

findings.summary: The http block for the 301 appears before the idea is stated, and the 'Cached redirects cannot be recalled' callout repeats pages 5 and 8.
findings.evidence: HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently ... Cache-Control: private, max-age=60
findings.fix: State the idea first and drop or shorten the repeated callout.

findings.summary: The cheatsheet repeats earlier pages at length instead of staying a short revision card, and the code generation section holds four dense bullets with multiple ideas each.
findings.evidence: Hash: first 7 chars of MD5/SHA-256 needs collision retry (salt, rehash) / Unique index on short_code is the last guard; insert-or-fail, never check-then-insert
findings.fix: Reduce to one row per strategy in a small table (strategy, collisions, guessable) and a single line for the unique-index rule.

findings.summary: Answers are long multi-clause bullets and one worked example repeats the explanation in several forms, so it is not scannable as an answer key.
findings.evidence: 3844 % 62 = 0, then 62 % 62 = 0, then 1 % 62 = 1; reversed, the remainders give 100
findings.fix: Show the steps as a small table of quotient and remainder, then give the final code on its own line.
